issues.summary: (MEDIUM) export_memories, which the docs present as a logical backup, omits the declared association graph, so a restore silently loses it. do_export_memories counts and streams only the memories, episodes and profiles tables (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:2591 and the bodies that follow), and do_import_memories dispatches only on the header, memory, episode and profile record types (3192-3225); anything else is an 'unknown type'. Entities, entity_aliases, entity_mentions and relations are declared data that the server cannot rebuild from content. An export, delete_agent_data and import round trip brings every memory back with ok:true but zero graph rows, and traverse then returns no_such_entity; neither response mentions the omission. merge_memories in copy mode likewise does not carry the graph to the target. docs/operations.md:30-33 recommends export/import as the logical backup with restore drills 'safe to rehearse', docs/tools.md:65 says the export 'doubles as a logical backup', and the runbook's list of what backups do not cover does not name the graph. The physical backup forms carry the graph intact, so loss needs the logical backup to be the one restored.
issues.fix_sketch: Extend the export format with entity, alias, mention and relation records keyed on export-local refs, and have import and merge (copy) remap them to the new memory and episode ids; merge (move) must carry the graph or refuse before deleting source rows. Until then, the export and import responses and docs/operations.md and docs/tools.md must state that the logical backup excludes declared associations.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10 and reproduced with an export, delete and import round trip. The fix needs an export format change, since mentions and relations are keyed on row ids that import reassigns.
issues.fix_note: export_memories now writes the declared graph after the records, as entity / mention / relation records keyed on the file's ids, with their counts in the header (format cpersona-export/1.1). import_memories maps every file record to the row it landed in, including a row skipped as already present. It then writes the graph through associations.carry with that map; this call is the anchored line. A cut graph section is refused by the header check. Files without graph records import as before. Reverting turns tests/test_2611a1_u01.py::test_export_import_round_trip_restores_the_declared_graph red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) A logical backup that export_memories writes can be refused by import_memories, and the refusal names a setting that does not exist. Import refuses files over 100 MiB with 'input file exceeds MAX_IMPORT_BYTES (104857600)' (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:2792, again at 3164), but the server reads the cap only from CPERSONA_MAX_IMPORT_BYTES (cpersona/config.py:85), and no doc page names either variable; setting MAX_IMPORT_BYTES changes nothing. Export has no matching cap, so a large corpus (sooner with include_embeddings=true or a larger embedding dimension) exports with ok:true and then cannot be restored along the documented path (docs/operations.md:30-33, docs/tools.md:65) until the operator reads config.py. No data is lost and a workaround exists.
issues.fix_sketch: Name CPERSONA_MAX_IMPORT_BYTES in both refusal messages and document it in docs/configuration.md. Have export warn when its output exceeds the import cap, or document the limit next to the backup and restore guidance in docs/operations.md.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10 and reproduced: a 110 MB export returned ok:true and the same file was refused on import. Related to bug-130.
issues.fix_note: The import size refusals name CPERSONA_MAX_IMPORT_BYTES, the variable config.py reads, and docs/configuration.md and operations.md (with their .ja.md pages) document the cap and that exports are not capped. tests/test_2611a2_w01.py::test_size_refusal_before_reading_names_the_env_setting (and ..._of_the_bounded_read_...) turns red if the message goes back to MAX_IMPORT_BYTES. test_import_cap_is_documented turns red if a page drops the variable.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) `import_memories` binds a JSON null in `msg_id`, `project_id`, `channel` or `timestamp` straight into NOT NULL columns. The values come from `record.get(...)` (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:2858-2860, 2896), and None gets past both dedup probes: `if msg_id:` is false, and `channel = NULL` never matches. The dry run therefore counts the row as imported. In the real run, `INSERT OR IGNORE INTO memories` (admin_handlers.py:2907) quietly drops the row on the NOT NULL constraint. The code then reaches `if cur.rowcount == 0:` (admin_handlers.py:2928) and adds it to `skipped_memories`, the duplicate counter, with no line in `errors`. The memory is lost while the response reads ok:true, and the preview disagrees with the real run without saying why. Episodes take the same defaults (admin_handlers.py:2998-2999), but they use a plain INSERT, so a null episode `channel` or `project_id` aborts and rolls back the whole restore, even though the preview had answered ok:true.
issues.fix_sketch: On both arms, coerce None to '' for `project_id`, `channel` and `msg_id`, and coerce or reject non-string timestamps, as bug-094 already does for episode keywords. Stop treating every `rowcount == 0` as a duplicate skip. For example, probe the dedup keys explicitly and report any other ignored insert as a per-line error.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10 and reproduced on a fresh database for memories with a null channel, project_id, timestamp or msg_id, and for an episode with a null channel. The same class as bug-094; bug-618 covers the other unconverted fields.
issues.fix_note: _null_as_empty reads a JSON null as the '' a missing key gets, before the dry_run split, for memory msg_id/project_id/channel/timestamp, episode project_id/channel and profile project_id/user_id; a non-string memory timestamp is a per-line error on both arms; an INSERT OR IGNORE that drops a row after both dedup probes is reported in errors instead of passing as a duplicate. Reverting turns red tests/test_2611a1_u02.py::test_null_memory_field_is_imported_on_both_arms, ::test_null_episode_axis_does_not_abort_the_restore, ::test_null_profile_key_does_not_abort_the_restore, ::test_non_string_memory_timestamp_is_a_per_line_error and ::test_an_insert_ignored_for_another_reason_is_not_a_silent_duplicate.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) `import_memories` overwrites a live profile that is newer than the file's copy. `_import_profile_record` does an unconditional `ON CONFLICT(agent_id, user_id) DO UPDATE SET content = excluded.content, updated_at = excluded.updated_at` (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:3093-3095). Since bug-223, `excluded.updated_at` is the record's own stamp. Re-importing an older export over a live database therefore replaces the newer profile text with the backup's and moves `updated_at` backwards. The response says only `profile_updated: true`, with no errors. Memories and episodes are deduplicated and skipped in the same situation. docs/operations.md:32-34 calls `import_memories` idempotent and says restore drills are safe to rehearse, which is not true for profiles. Repeating the same import does leave the same state, so the tool description's idempotence claim (keyed on memories and episodes) still holds. Only an operator can trigger this, and the profile is a derived summary that can be regenerated.
issues.pattern: ^        if stored_time is not None and stored_time > file_time:$
issues.fix_sketch: First decide what a restore should do with a profile that is newer than the file's. Then either keep the live row when its `updated_at` is newer and report a per-line skip, or keep the overwrite and say so in the response with both stamps. Either way, correct docs/operations.md:32-34.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10 and reproduced on a fresh database. The fix needs a contract decision on restore semantics for profiles; the updated_at carry-over comes from bug-223 (see also bug-620).
issues.fix_note: _import_profile_record probes the stored profile's updated_at on both arms and keeps the stored row, with a per-line errors entry and profile_updated left false, when it is strictly newer than the file's parsed stamp; otherwise the upsert applies as before (bug-223 stamp carry kept). Reverting turns red tests/test_2611a1_u02.py::test_restore_drill_keeps_the_newer_stored_profile.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) `import_memories` collects one error string per bad line with no cap and returns the whole list. Lines that fail to parse (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:3187), records with an unknown `_type`, and records that lack `agent_id` (admin_handlers.py:3203, 3211, 3219, 3225) each append a message to `tally.errors`. The full list goes out on both the success path (admin_handlers.py:3268) and the abort path (admin_handlers.py:3247). The only bound is the 100 MiB MAX_IMPORT_BYTES input cap. A dry-run preview of a 3 MB file of 1,000,000 short non-JSON lines returned ok:true with one million error strings: a 72 MB response, 24 times the input size. At the input cap, the same pattern extrapolates to a response of roughly 2.4 GB and several GB of memory, so pointing the tool at the wrong file can exhaust the process or flood the client.
issues.fix_sketch: Cap `tally.errors` at the first N messages and add an `errors_truncated` count. Consider aborting early when none of the first K lines parses as an export record. Return the same bounded shape on the abort and success paths.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10 and reproduced with a 3 MB dry-run preview. bug-130 and bug-241 bound only the input bytes, not the error list.
issues.fix_note: _ImportErrors keeps the first 100 import error messages and counts the rest, and the response ends with '<N> more errors were not listed' on both the success and abort paths. tests/test_2611a2_w01.py::test_import_error_list_is_bounded_on_success turns red (5000 messages for 5000 bad lines) if tally.errors goes back to an unbounded list.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The bug-218 guard that makes a move delete only the copied profiles and episodes (`_MOVE_DELETE_SQL`, cpersona/admin_handlers.py:3553-3554) has no test that mixes copied and skipped rows in one move. The existing bug-218 test copies zero profiles, so the chunk loop in `_delete_merged_source_rows` (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:3594-3598) never runs a DELETE, and the other test copies every row. Reproduced by mutation: turning the id-keyed profile (or episode) delete into a whole-agent delete keeps the suite green, while a move that copies one profile and skips another then destroys the skipped profile, which exists nowhere else. That is the bug-218 data loss coming back undetected. The memories variant is caught by the merge-move golden; the production code is correct today.
issues.pattern: \("deleted_profiles", "DELETE FROM profiles WHERE agent_id = \? AND id IN \(\{ph\}\)"\),
issues.fix_sketch: Extend the bug-218 test, and add an episode equivalent, so one move both copies and skips rows; assert that only the copied ids are deleted (deleted count 1, left_at_source 1) and that the skipped source row survives.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10; reproduced by a mutation probe (test-only, the shipped code is correct). Guards the fix for bug-218.
issues.fix_note: Test-only: pins the id-keyed profile delete of a move. tests/test_2611a2_w01.py::test_move_keeps_the_skipped_profile_when_another_is_copied (and the episode twin test_move_keeps_the_skipped_episode_when_another_is_copied for the episodes line) turns red if the delete stops being restricted to copied ids (deleted_profiles == 2).

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) Operator edits to the alias ledger that change or remove an existing row are not honored by a running server, so a wrong cross-subject link the operator meant to undo keeps working. `resolve_or_issue` answers a hit from the in-memory snapshot without consulting the file (cpersona/aliases.py:139-140), and the re-read happens only on a miss (cpersona/aliases.py:149); a relink of a pair the process already holds is ignored until some unrelated subject's miss or a restart. `_merged_with_disk` starts from the snapshot and only adds or overwrites rows from disk (cpersona/aliases.py:215-219), so a row the operator deleted stays live in memory and the next issuance for any other subject writes it back through `_persist` (cpersona/aliases.py:164, 257), where it survives a restart with nothing logged. Both variants were reproduced with a probe. The relink staleness heals at the next miss; the resurrected deletion does not. It needs an operator mistake plus an edit made while the server runs, but docs/OAUTH_DESIGN.md describes the ledger as operator-editable without mentioning a restart.
issues.fix_sketch: On a miss, rebuild from the file plus only this call's new row instead of taking the union with the snapshot, and re-validate hits against the file's mtime or fingerprint (or offer an explicit reload); otherwise document that edits require a restart.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10; reproduced by a probe. Incomplete fix of bug-351, whose fix assumed ledger rows are only ever added; related to bug-630.
issues.fix_note: AliasLedger._refresh replaces the in-memory rows wholesale with the file whenever its fingerprint changed (no union with the startup snapshot), and peek, issued_aliases and resolve_or_issue all call it, so an operator's relink or removal takes effect on the next call and is not resurrected by a later issuance. Reverting turns tests/test_2611a1_u16.py::test_bug531_an_operator_relink_takes_effect_on_the_next_call and ::test_bug531_a_removed_row_is_neither_served_nor_written_back red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) A record ref or id beyond SQLite's signed 64-bit range escapes as OverflowError instead of being reported as a malformed item, and on `store` this happens after the memory has already committed. `parse_ref` accepts any digit run and converts it unchecked (cpersona/associations.py:59, :73), and `_record_exists` binds it straight into SQL (associations.py:115-119). In `do_store_boundary` the associations rider (cpersona/server.py:297-304) and the lock rider (server.py:309-316) run after `do_store` committed the row, with no exception handling, so the MCP layer answers a bare `{"error": "Python int too large to convert to SQLite INTEGER"}` with no `result` or `id`. Reproduced through the MCP request handler on a fresh database: a store with `lock: true` and a relation subject `mem:99999999999999999999` left the row stored with locked=0, the valid entity declared in the same call was rolled back, and every retry answered the same error; the in-range control reports the bad ref in `associations.dropped` and stores and locks the memory as documented. The same unbounded id also turns into a bare error in `declare_associations` (via `anchor_ref` or a retract id), in `get_contents` (one bad ref fails the whole batch), and in the id-taking tools (`delete_memory`, `update_memory`, `lock_memory`, and others). The same unguarded post-commit riders also turn a lock-contention failure into a bare error for a committed write; that variant was reported but not re-run.
issues.pattern: return \(m\.group\(1\), row_id\) if fits_sqlite_integer\(row_id\) else None
issues.fix_sketch: Range-check parsed ids in `parse_ref` and `_is_id` (0 < id <= 2**63-1) so an oversized ref is dropped like any other malformed item, and apply the same bound in retract, `get_contents` and the id-taking tools. Wrap the post-commit riders in `do_store_boundary` so a rider failure is reported next to `result` and `id` (an associations error, `locked: false`) instead of replacing the response.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10; reproduced. Related: bug-447 (the earlier `_is_id` bool fix), bug-533 (the same oversized id in retract), bug-631 (a race that reaches the same post-commit rider failure).
issues.fix_note: parse_ref and _is_id refuse ids outside SQLite's signed 64-bit range (utils.fits_sqlite_integer), _endpoint drops a ref-shaped value parse_ref refuses instead of registering it as an entity name, get_contents and delete_memory/update_memory/lock_memory/unlock_memory/delete_episode answer not-found before binding, and do_store_boundary guards both post-commit riders so a failure is reported in associations.dropped / locked:false next to result and id. Reverting turns the store-rider, declare/retract, get_contents, by-id and rider-fault tests in tests/test_2611a1_u13.py red with OverflowError / database is locked.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) `declare_associations` bounds its declarations by `MAX_ITEMS`, but its `retract` lists are unbounded, contrary to the module docstring's promise that the whole call is bounded (cpersona/associations.py:27-28). `retract()` loops over every relation id and every mention, issuing one DELETE each inside a single `transaction()` (associations.py:339-357), which holds the process-wide write lock (cpersona/database.py:347); the tool schema gives `retract.relations` and `retract.mentions` no `maxItems` (cpersona/server.py:1162-1175). Reproduced through the real MCP handler: a 689 KB call with 100,000 relation ids held the write lock for 4.6 s and blocked a store by a different agent for 4.44 s, with nothing reported as dropped. A second variant was also reproduced: `_is_id` (associations.py:87-89) accepts an id of 2**63, the DELETE raises OverflowError, the whole retract rolls back (a valid relation id in the same list stays), and the caller gets a bare `{"error": ...}` even though the declare half of the call had already committed in its own transaction. The damage stays within the caller's own rows; the cross-agent effect is the write stall.
issues.fix_sketch: Apply `MAX_ITEMS` to `retract.relations` and `retract.mentions`, both in the handler (reporting the excess in `dropped`) and as `maxItems` in the schema. Have `_is_id` reject values outside the signed 64-bit range so they are reported in `dropped` rather than raised.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10; reproduced. Related: bug-447 (`_is_id`), bug-532 (the same oversized-id OverflowError through refs and the store rider). The out-of-range id variant is fixed in 2.6.11a1: _is_id rejects an id outside SQLite's integer range, so it is reported in dropped instead of raising (bug-532). The unbounded retract lists are not.
issues.fix_note: retract() cuts relations and mentions at MAX_ITEMS through _retract_list before the write transaction: items past the bound are reported in dropped ('beyond the 64-item bound') and never deleted, and a non-list retract list is reported as 'must be a list'. Reverting turns the four retract tests in tests/test_2611a2_w03.py red (66 retracted instead of 64; 10000 DELETEs instead of 128).

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The relation walk in reconstruct drops evidence for an entity that another chosen item mentions, so what the walk adds to an item depends on `count`. `walk_graph` runs one breadth-first search from the union of every chosen item's mentioned entities, all at distance 0 (cpersona/associations.py:693-694, :538), and loads mentioning records only for entities at distance >= 1 (associations.py:704). The per-item walk in reconstruct.py then recomputes distances per cluster, so item A can reach an entity at hop 1, but that entity has no loaded records because item B mentions it and made it a union start. Reproduced on a fresh database: a record attached to item A as walked evidence at `count=1` disappeared from every item at `count=2`, with no `bounds.omitted` entry. This contradicts the comment at cpersona/reconstruct.py:1666-1669 and docs/ASSOCIATIVE_MEMORY_DESIGN.md section 9 ("what it adds to an item does not depend on `count`"). It needs only two candidates whose mentioned entities are joined by a relation, which is common around a shared hub entity; it does not corrupt or leak data.
issues.fix_sketch: In `walk_graph`, fetch records for every entity within `max_hops`, including the union starts that another item can reach at hop >= 1, or run the neighbourhood per cluster. Keep excluding each item's own hop-0 entities in the per-item walk, which it already does.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10; reproduced. Related: bug-635 (the same record-loading loop reads more than it returns).
issues.fix_note: walk_graph reads mentioning records for every entity some start ref reaches through at least one relation within max_hops (each start's own reach followed over the loaded adjacency), not only entities at distance >= 1 from the union of all starts, so an entity another chosen item mentions still yields evidence. Reverting turns the four bug-534 tests in tests/test_2611a2_w03.py red (graph.records == {}, item a loses its walked record at count=2).

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) Two block index builds of the same file share fixed temp paths, so overlapping builds can publish a torn index that still loads and reads as current. `build_block_index` uses `{out}.tmp` and `{out}.bits.tmp` (cpersona/block_index.py:264), opened with O_CREAT and O_TRUNC but no O_EXCL; it streams rows into the bits file with awaits between pages, copies it into the temp file by name (block_index.py:394-395), and its `finally` unlinks both names whichever build created them (block_index.py:271-276). A second build truncating the bits file mid-stream leaves a zero-filled hole; the first build publishes it with `os.replace`, the size check in `load_block_index` (block_index.py:443-445) passes, the header's clock marks it current so no rebuild is due, the change log is pruned, and recall serves the wrong bits for unchanged records until about 35,000 further changes (`LIVE_ROW_BOUND`, block_index.py:83); the other build fails with FileNotFoundError. Overlap happens when two server processes on one database each run their own task queue and both execute the same unclaimed `block_index_build` row (`_fetch_next`, cpersona/tasks.py:389-397), or when an operator runs `python -m cpersona.block_index build` while the server builds. Reproduced in-process and across processes: published, loadable, current files held wrong (all-zero) bits for up to 71% of rows. SQLite data is intact and deleting the file repairs it. `vector_index.py:361` and `coarse_index.py:186` use the same fixed temp-name pattern.
issues.fix_sketch: Give each build its own temp files (O_EXCL, or mkstemp in the output directory) and clean up only the names this build created; optionally serialise builds per output file with an advisory lock so a duplicate queue execution is a no-op. Apply the same treatment to the vector and coarse index builders.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10; reproduced. This is the shared-temp-file class of bug-350 recurring in an index builder.
issues.fix_note: build_block_index creates both temp files with mkstemp in the output directory (new fileperms.temp_beside) and in its finally removes only the names it created. A concurrent build can no longer truncate, interleave or unlink them. issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The block divider is quadratic on text with many unclosed brackets. The first pass of `_bracket_depth` (cpersona/blocks.py:157-166) walks the whole stack of pending openers (`for depth in range(len(pending) - 1, -1, -1)`, line 162) for every character that is not an opener, whether or not it can close anything, so the cost is O(unclosed openers x characters). `_structural_cuts` also tests every boundary match against every fence range (`any(a < end < b for a, b in protected)`, line 191), which is quadratic in the number of code fences. `segment()` runs synchronously on the event loop, at read time from excerpts.py:116 and reconstruct.py:1296 and at write time in the block build. Reproduced: doubling a record of unclosed openers from 8k to 16k characters raised the time 4.3x (241 ms to 1026 ms), against 8 ms for 16k characters of prose, so a few stored records of this shape can stall every client's recall or reconstruct for seconds.
issues.pattern: by_closer: dict\[str, list\[int\]\] = \{closer: \[\] for closer in _BRACKETS\.values\(\)\}
issues.fix_sketch: Make the unmatched-opener pass linear by keeping, per closer type, a stack of indices of pending openers so a non-matching character costs O(1), and use bisect over the sorted fence ranges in `_structural_cuts`. Optionally move `segment()` off the event loop with `asyncio.to_thread`.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10 and reproduced with a timing probe. The stack scan came in with the fix for bug-473.
issues.fix_note: _bracket_depth finds the nearest matching opening through a stack per closing bracket (linear, each opening leaves the stacks once), and _structural_cuts finds the one fence range that can hold a boundary by bisection over the sorted, disjoint ranges instead of testing every fence. Reverting either makes tests/test_2611a2_w04.py::test_division_of_a_pathological_record_costs_what_prose_costs go red (unclosed-openers/stray-closers for the bracket pass, fences for the fence test); test_the_linear_divider_draws_the_same_cuts_as_the_rule pins that the cuts are unchanged.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The compare-and-swap that block and node writes rely on runs outside the SQLite transaction. `write_blocks` (cpersona/blocks.py:631) and `write_nodes` (cpersona/nodes.py:319) check that the parent text is unchanged with a plain SELECT, and `_parent_row`'s docstring (blocks.py:434-437) says that read happens inside the write's own transaction. It does not: `transaction()` (cpersona/database.py:324-357) never issues a BEGIN, so under sqlite3's deferred mode the SELECT runs in autocommit and the implicit transaction only starts at the following DELETE, on a fresh snapshot, so no busy-snapshot error can catch a commit in the gap. Reproduced with a second connection committing right after the check: a deleted parent left block rows and vectors (and node rows) behind, an edited parent got blocks spanning text it no longer holds, and the write still returned True; with BEGIN IMMEDIATE the outside commit was refused. Reaching it needs several processes on one database file, a supported deployment; the orphaned rows are never returned by recall or get_contents, so the damage is wasted rows and stale derived text rather than exposure.
issues.fix_sketch: Run the CAS read and the DELETE/INSERTs in one write transaction opened with BEGIN IMMEDIATE, either in `transaction()` or before the read in `write_blocks`/`write_nodes`. Separately add an orphan sweep for record_blocks, record_block_vectors and record_nodes to the health check so rows already written can be found and removed.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10 and reproduced with a two-connection race probe; the claimed HIGH was lowered because it needs a multi-process deployment and the orphans are not readable. Same CAS family as bug-490.
issues.fix_note: write_blocks (and write_nodes in cpersona/nodes.py, same line) now call database.hold_write_lock(db) before the compare-and-swap read; the helper issues BEGIN IMMEDIATE when the transaction() body has not written yet (no-op when it has, so a health repair run that writes nodes then blocks joins one transaction). The read and the DELETE/INSERTs share one write transaction, so a commit from another process waits or is refused instead of landing in the gap. Reverting it turns tests/test_2611a1_u08.py::test_write_blocks_delete_cannot_land_between_check_and_write (and the edit, build_blocks and write_nodes race tests) red with 'block rows and vectors written for deleted memory ... outside commit: committed'.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) Block backfill's guard against a down embedding backend never fires when the swept range holds any single-block record. The guard at cpersona/blocks.py:1045 raises only when `failed and not (built or needed_none or refused)`, but `needed_none` is incremented on the offline path for every record that divides into one block (blocks.py:1003-1013), which needs no backend and says nothing about whether it is up. With the backend down, a page holding one short and one long memory therefore advances the cursor past the failed record (lines 1032-1033) and reports 'backfill swept the corpus' instead of raising so the queue retries the same cursor; reproduced with a client whose embed raises (removing the short memory restores the raise). The failed multi-block records stay without blocks for the life of the process. The only test (tests/test_blocks_backfill.py:396-410) seeds multi-block records only.
issues.pattern: if failed and not \(built or refused\):
issues.fix_sketch: Base the outage test only on outcomes that needed the backend, for example `failed and not (built or refused)`, or count the offline single-block case separately from the 'none' that `_build_one` returns. Add a test that seeds a single-block record next to multi-block ones.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10 and reproduced with a down-backend probe. The offline single-block path that defeats the guard is the fix for bug-498.
issues.fix_note: The backfill's outage guard counts only outcomes that reached the embedding backend (built, refused); records that need no blocks are decided offline and no longer mask an outage. Reverting to include needed_none makes tests/test_2611a2_w04.py::test_an_outage_raises_even_when_the_corpus_holds_a_single_block_record fail with DID NOT RAISE.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) Health and deep-check repairs that delete or rewrite memories never update the remote vector index in remote vector mode. The duplicate_content repair (cpersona/checks.py:274), the empty_content delete (checks.py:2293-2296), the collision delete in `_rewrite_or_delete_on_collision` (checks.py:158-166) and deep_short_content (checks.py:3818-3820) delete rows locally, and the annotation, mention and oversized-content repairs rewrite content locally, but neither `do_check_health` nor `do_deep_check` posts a /remove or /index, unlike `do_delete_memory` and `do_update_memory`, which use `_post_remote_side_effect` (admin_handlers.py:475, 563). Reproduced: after check_health(fix=true) removed a duplicate and rewrote an annotated row, the remote index still held a vector for the deleted id and the old-text vector for the rewritten one, so later remote searches can spend a top-K slot on a row that rehydrates to nothing or score a row on text it no longer holds.
issues.fix_sketch: Have the deleting fixers return the ids they removed and the rewriting fixers return the rewritten (id, text). After the transaction commits, `do_check_health` and `do_deep_check` post /remove and /index through the same `_post_remote_side_effect` helper the delete and update handlers use.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10 and reproduced against a stand-in remote index. Same class as the handler-level remote syncs added for bug-023, bug-011 and bug-346, and the remote side of bug-028.
issues.fix_note: The deleting and rewriting repairs (duplicate_content, empty_content, collision deletes and rewrites in memory_annotation/discord_mention/oversized_content, deep short_content) record (owner, id, new text or None) in checks.remote_index_effects while in the write transaction; a check rolled back to its savepoint drops its records; after the commit do_check_health and do_deep_check post the net state through _sync_remote_index -> admin_handlers._post_remote_side_effect (/remove and /index, chunked at 128). Reverting turns tests/test_2611a1_u07.py::test_health_repairs_update_the_remote_index and ::test_deep_short_content_removes_from_the_remote_index red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The duplicate_content repair can delete the only copy a channel-scoped reader can see. The survivor rule at cpersona/checks.py:261-268 keeps `COALESCE(MIN(CASE WHEN channel = '' THEN id END), MIN(id))` per (agent_id, project_id, content) group and line 274 deletes every other unlocked row, so a group with no channel '' row keeps the lowest id and deletes copies in sibling channels. A recall scoped to channel X reads only X and '' (isolation.py:104-106), so that reader loses the memory. Reproduced: the same text stored in chanA and chanB, check_health(fix=true) reported healthy and left only the chanA row, and a chanB-scoped recall went from one result to none; storing the text in chanB again then succeeds, so the store path and the repair disagree about what a duplicate is. Channel is not an isolation boundary, the text survives in the other channel and in unscoped reads, and a dry run lists the group, so there is no cross-tenant exposure; the defect is the contract conflict and the lost channel-scoped visibility.
issues.fix_sketch: Delete a sibling-channel copy only when a channel '' survivor in the same group still covers that channel's readers; a group with no '' row should be reported and left alone, or collapsed per channel. Once the policy is chosen, align the detection grouping, the survivor rule, the `_insert_dup` test framing and the comment at checks.py:229-240 with the store contract.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10 and reproduced end to end; the claimed HIGH was lowered. The fix needs a policy decision because cross-channel cleanup was an intentional, test-pinned choice (bug-014, bug-128).
issues.fix_note: duplicate_content selects as surplus only rows covered for their channel's readers: an older row in the same (agent, project, channel, content) bucket, or, for a named-channel row, a channel='' row with the same agent, project and content. Detection, repairable COUNT and DELETE share that predicate. Reverting to the MIN(id) fallback survivor turns tests/test_2611a1_u09.py::test_sibling_channel_copy_survives_duplicate_repair and ::test_store_and_repair_agree_on_what_a_duplicate_is red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The agent-scoped keyset scan in `check_nonfinite_embedding` is quadratic. The page query at cpersona/checks.py:401-406 (`WHERE embedding IS NOT NULL AND id > ? AND agent_id = ? ORDER BY id LIMIT 100`) is served by SQLite from idx_memories_msg_id(agent_id, msg_id), which is not ordered by id, so every 100-row page reads every embedded row the agent has and sorts it in a temp B-tree. Reproduced: four times the rows took 14.4 times as long for a scoped call, while the unscoped call walks the rowid range and stays linear. Under fix=true the scan runs inside `transaction()`, so all writers wait on the write lock for its duration. The merge copy passes use the same query shape (admin_handlers.py:3331 for memories, 3428 for episodes).
issues.pattern: SELECT id, embedding FROM .table. NOT INDEXED
issues.fix_sketch: Make the planner walk the rowid range, for example with `+agent_id = ?` as vector.py:851 already does, or add an index on (agent_id, id) that serves ORDER BY id. Apply the same change to the merge page queries and add a regression test asserting the scoped page's plan has no temp B-tree.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10 and reproduced with timings and EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN. The paging came in with the fix for bug-358.
issues.fix_note: The non-finite embedding scan reads its keyset pages NOT INDEXED, and the merge copy passes spell their agent term +agent_id, so each page walks the primary key instead of sorting the whole agent per page. Reverting turns tests/test_2611a2_w05.py::test_scoped_nonfinite_scan_pages_without_sorting_the_agent (checks.py) or ::test_merge_pages_walk_the_primary_key (admin_handlers.py) red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) In remote vector mode an embedding fault latched by maintenance probes is never cleared, so every recall carries a false degraded advisory until restart. `probe_embedding_dim` and `prefetch_null_embeddings` report failures to the health breaker but never success (cpersona/checks.py:621-625, 790-793), leaving recovery to the recall path. In remote mode a recall answered by /search returns at cpersona/vector.py:1969-1973, before the local embed and before the only `health.observe_ok()` call (vector.py:2009). Reproduced: two check_health(fix=true) runs while /embed was down latched the fault; after the service recovered, recalls returned results through the remote index yet still carried the 'fell back to keyword/FTS-only' advisory (memory_handlers.py:3173), and the fault stayed latched.
issues.pattern: ^        health\.observe_ok\(\)  # the remote /search answer reached the service$
issues.fix_sketch: Count a successful remote /search, which uses the same embedding service, as an attempted success and call `observe_ok`. Alternatively let a maintenance probe that actually reached the backend clear the fault, revisiting the bug-129 choice that recovery stays with recall for the case where recall never embeds.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10 and reproduced with a remote-mode probe. Related to bug-274 and bug-129; see also bug-543, which reports the same latch from the health check's side.
issues.fix_note: vector._search_vector calls health.observe_ok() when the remote /search returns an authoritative answer, so a fault latched by maintenance probes clears in remote mode once the service answers again. Reverting it turns tests/test_2611a2_w07.py::test_remote_search_answer_clears_a_fault_latched_by_maintenance red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) check_embedding_backend reports the backend unreachable even when its own probe on this run reached it. At cpersona/checks.py:686-690 a non-None probed dimension falls into the else branch, which reads `health.is_faulted()`; the comment there says 'Nothing probed on this run', but the branch also covers a successful probe with `dim_probe_reached_backend` True, and `probe_embedding_dim` (checks.py:603-634) never clears the fault. `prefetch_null_embeddings` also returns early while the fault is latched (checks.py:763-764), so the fix run cannot re-embed. Reproduced: after a latched fault and a recovered backend, do_check_health(fix=True) reported embedding_backend_unreachable, status degraded, and the fault stayed latched, so the hint to re-run the check to confirm recovery cannot be satisfied from this surface.
issues.pattern: elif embedding_cache is not None and reached_backend:
issues.fix_sketch: When `dim_probe_reached_backend` is True and a dimension came back, report connected (or a recovered-but-latched state) instead of reading `is_faulted()`. Alternatively let a probe that reached the backend re-arm the breaker so the prefetch can backfill in the same run.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10 and reproduced with a backend-switching probe. Related to bug-274 and bug-248; in remote vector mode this combines with bug-542 so the latch can never clear.
issues.fix_note: check_embedding_backend lets a probe on this run that reached the backend and returned a vector outrank a latched fault (connected), and do_check_health runs the probe before the prefetch and passes backend_answered so prefetch_null_embeddings backfills under the latch. Reverting the branch turns tests/test_2611a2_w06.py::test_a_probe_that_reached_the_backend_is_not_overruled_by_a_latched_fault red; reverting the prefetch bypass turns test_a_restarted_backend_is_confirmed_and_backfilled_by_one_fix_run red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) With an in-memory database, the report-only FTS integrity probe rolls back a concurrent writer's uncommitted statements. For ':memory:' the read seam returns the write connection (cpersona/database.py:988-991). do_check_health with fix=False runs its checks under `connection()`, not under the write lock (maintenance_handlers.py:148-151), and check_fts_integrity then calls `release_read_probe_transaction` (checks.py:1074-1076), which rolls back whenever `in_transaction` is True (database.py:202-204), here the open transaction of another coroutine's `transaction()`. The writer continues, commits only its later statements and reports success. Reproduced: a two-row write reported committed with one row stored, and an import reported 400 rows with 118 stored; guarding the helper with `if db is _db: return False` made all three tests pass. In-memory mode is not the shipped default and its data is ephemeral, and the trigger needs a report-only health run to interleave with a multi-statement write.
issues.fix_sketch: Make `release_read_probe_transaction` return early when the connection is the write connection, the same aliasing guard `connection()`'s exit already has, or have check_fts_integrity skip the release when the read seam aliases the writer.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10 and reproduced, including a mutation run with the guard added; the claimed HIGH was lowered because only in-memory deployments reach it. The release helper was added by the fix for bug-314.
issues.fix_note: release_read_probe_transaction returns without rolling back when the probe ran on the write connection, which happens only with an in-memory database, while transaction() holds the write lock. The open transaction then belongs to that writer, and its commit ends the probe's statement too. With the lock free it still releases the probe's own transaction. Reverting it turns tests/test_2611a1_u03.py::test_bug544_report_only_fts_probe_keeps_a_concurrent_writers_statements red (1 of 2 acknowledged rows stored).

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) axis_hygiene reports unrelated non-ASCII project_ids as naming drift. The drift key is built with `_PROJECT_ID_NORMALIZE = re.compile(r"[^a-z0-9]")` (cpersona/checks.py:1763) applied after lower() (:1789), so every id written entirely in CJK or another non-Latin script collapses to the empty key, and ids that differ only in non-ASCII characters collapse onto the ASCII they share. Reproduced on a fresh DB: two pairs of unrelated project_ids, two written entirely in Japanese and two that share only the suffix '2025' after Japanese words, were each reported as one project_id_naming_drift cluster, and status came back 'degraded'. The check is registered warn and not fix-capable (:3496), so the status stays degraded and `checkup --strict` exits 1 for as long as both buckets exist; the only way out is renaming projects to ASCII. project_id accepts free text, and no doc restricts it to ASCII.
issues.fix_sketch: Normalize with a Unicode-aware fold that keeps letters and digits from every script (for example NFKC plus casefold, then drop separators such as -_. and whitespace), and never cluster ids whose key is empty.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10; reproduced on a fresh database. Related: bug-243 (scoping of the same check).
issues.fix_note: The project_id drift key is NFKC + casefold, keeping letters, digits and combining marks of every script, and an empty key never clusters. Before, it kept only [a-z0-9], so ids in other scripts collapsed together. Reverting turns tests/test_2611a2_w05.py::test_axis_hygiene_does_not_fold_other_scripts_together and ::test_axis_hygiene_still_reports_drift_in_any_script red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) invalid_timestamp decides validity with SQLite datetime(), which rejects ISO-8601 forms the rest of the package reads, and its repair overwrites them with the insertion time. cpersona/checks.py:1871 counts rows where `datetime(timestamp) IS NULL`, and the fix at :1897-1904 sets timestamp from created_at on the same predicate. The store path keeps the caller's stamp verbatim (cpersona/memory_handlers.py:199), and the Python readers (`_parse_timestamp_utc`, cpersona/utils.py:153-171, and `_classify_timestamp`) accept a colonless offset ('+0900'), a bare-hour offset ('+09') and basic format ('20250102T100000Z'). Reproduced: a row stored as '2025-01-02T10:00:00+0900' was reported as invalid_timestamp (and as repairable timestamp_format_drift), and check_health(fix=True) replaced it with its created_at, losing the 2025 event time for good; a control spelled with '+09:00' was normalised without loss. invalid_timestamp is registered before timestamp_format_drift (:3498 vs :3508), so the destructive repair wins over the lossless one. Loss needs both a non-colon form from the client and an explicit fix run by a writer on that agent, and stays inside the caller's isolation scope. A future stamp in these forms is also invisible to check_future_timestamp (:1949), though invalid_timestamp catches it.
issues.pattern: canon = _sqlite_readable_stamp\(ts\) if isinstance\(ts, str\) else None
issues.fix_sketch: Decide validity with the same parser the readers use and rewrite any stamp Python can read to its canonical UTC '+00:00' form, keeping the created_at fallback only for stamps nothing can parse. Better still, normalise caller stamps at the store seam so SQLite datetime() and strftime() see one form.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10; reproduced end to end on a fresh database. Reported as HIGH and lowered to MEDIUM: no cross-agent reach, needs a non-default timestamp form plus an explicit fix run. Related: bug-229 (the canonical form the repair writes), bug-547 (the same repair leaves the coarse index stale).
issues.fix_note: check_invalid_timestamp first respells each unlocked stamp that SQLite's datetime() rejects but utils._parse_timestamp_utc reads. Aware stamps become canonical UTC and naive ones stay naive, the result is confirmed readable by SQLite, and the rewrite runs before the created_at fallback, which now catches only stamps nothing can parse. If this is reverted, tests/test_2611a1_u10.py::test_invalid_timestamp_fix_keeps_the_instant_of_a_readable_stamp goes red, as do full_fix_run_keeps_event_time and naive_readable_stamp_stays_naive.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The coarse index filters a time-cue period against timestamps snapshotted at build time, and the health repairs that rewrite timestamps never mark it stale. cpersona/coarse_index.py:147-162 stores each row's datetime(timestamp) (NUL bytes when unreadable), and cpersona/coarse_search.py:256-257 compares the period against that snapshot; the only freshness probes are a cleared embedding and a deleted row. check_future_timestamp (cpersona/checks.py:1969-1977) and check_invalid_timestamp (:1897-1904) rewrite memories.timestamp from created_at in place. Reproduced: after a build, a row stamped 2099 and a row stamped 'not a time' were repaired into March 2026; SQL and the live supplier placed both in a March period (one was the exact match), while the index supplier used by the default cue mode omitted both, and check_coarse_index returned no finding on the stale file. Repaired rows go missing from the vector half of cue recalls until an unprompted rebuild, contrary to the module contract that both suppliers return the same candidates (coarse_search.py:23-32). The scan-position differences are partly by design.
issues.pattern: if index is None or not np\.isin\(np\.asarray\(ids, dtype=np\.int64\), index\.ids\)\.any\(\):
issues.fix_sketch: Have the timestamp repairs mark the coarse index stale, for example by recording the repaired ids or bumping a generation that _from_index checks and then falling back or reading those rows exactly. Alternatively, have check_coarse_index compare the stored stamps of indexed rows with live datetime(timestamp) and report or rebuild on drift.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10; reproduced on a fresh database. Related: bug-546 (the invalid_timestamp repair), bug-549 (check_coarse_index does not rebuild when it finds no issue).
issues.fix_note: The invalid_timestamp and future_timestamp repairs select the ids they are about to rewrite and call the new coarse_index.discard_if_holding. It removes the derived coarse index (as a purge does) when the file holds any of those ids, because the file's build-time datetime(timestamp) copy would otherwise drop the record from its new period. If the call in check_invalid_timestamp or check_future_timestamp is reverted, the matching parameter of tests/test_2611a1_u06.py::test_a_timestamp_repair_does_not_leave_the_coarse_index_answering_from_the_old_stamp fails. If the holding check is removed, test_a_timestamp_repair_of_a_record_the_index_does_not_hold_keeps_the_file fails.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The anonymous_source hint sends the reader to an unscoped deep_check(fix=true), which also deletes every short memory of that agent. cpersona/checks.py:2582 says 'Use deep_check with fix=true to recover names from content' without naming checks=['anonymous_source']. deep_check with no checks runs the whole deep registry (cpersona/maintenance_handlers.py:325), and with fix=true deep_short_content deletes every unlocked memory of the agent whose trimmed content is 5 characters or less (cpersona/checks.py:3800-3821, threshold at :138). Reproduced on a fresh database: following the hint literally recovered the anonymous name and in the same call deleted an unrelated memory that states a complete fact in five Japanese characters. Neither the hint nor the check_health response warns about the deletion.
issues.fix_sketch: Make the hint name the scoped call, deep_check(agent_id, fix=true, checks=['anonymous_source']). Separately, state in the deep_check description that the short_content repair deletes rows, or have the hint recommend a dry run first.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10; reproduced on a fresh database. Related: bug-015 (locked rows survive the short-content repair).
issues.fix_note: The anonymous_source hint names the scoped call deep_check(agent_id, fix=true, checks=['anonymous_source']), so following it repairs attribution without running the short_content deletion; the deep_check description also states that the short_content repair deletes rows. Reverting the hint turns tests/test_2611a1_u09.py::test_following_the_anonymous_source_hint_deletes_nothing_else red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The bug-315 rows-missing detection in check_vector_index and check_coarse_index is masked by rows the index never held. Both compare `index.count` with a live `COUNT(*) WHERE id <= watermark AND embedding IS NOT NULL` (cpersona/checks.py:2834-2841 and :3016-3023). index.count is only the kept rows (cpersona/vector_index.py:274), but the live count also includes the build's excluded_ids (embedded rows with a non-canonical created_at, for example an imported '2025-01-01T00:00:00Z') and unembedded_ids whose NULL embedding the routine null_embedding repair filled after the build. Each such row hides one deleted indexed row. Reproduced: on an all-canonical store, deleting one indexed row is reported by both checks; with one excluded row, or one hole filled after the build, the same deletion leaves live_indexed equal to index.count and both checks return no finding. Reads stay correct because the index falls back to the scan, but the latency and the skipped coarse remainder the finding exists to surface go unreported. In addition, check_coarse_index returns before its fix branch when no issue is found (:3042-3043 vs :3056), although its docstring says fix rebuilds 'whatever the state' (:2922), so the remainder hint's suggested fix=true is a no-op in this state.
issues.pattern: WHERE id <= \? AND embedding IS NOT NULL
issues.fix_sketch: Count live rows among the ids the index actually holds, for example by subtracting the live rows in excluded_ids and unembedded_ids or by checking index.ids for existence in bounded chunks, in both checks. Make check_coarse_index's fix=true rebuild even when no issue is found, as its docstring states.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10; reproduced with a control on fresh databases. The anchor is the vector_index count; the coarse twin is the same query on `memories` in check_coarse_index. Related: bug-315 (the detection this completes), bug-642 (the same counts are not agent-scoped).
issues.fix_note: Fixed by removal with bug-514. Neither check compares index.count with a live count any more: a deleted row is named by the vector change log and read through it, so it no longer sends a read to the scan or the live store, and the state in which a read is sent there -- a log that cannot vouch for the file -- is reported as vector_index_log_refused / coarse_index_log_refused, which the build's named holes cannot mask. check_coarse_index's docstring no longer claims that fix rebuilds in a state it does not report.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) check_health(fix=true) builds the coarse index while holding the shared write lock. `check_coarse_index` is fix-capable (cpersona/checks.py:3521) and not in `WHOLE_DB_SCAN_CHECKS` (checks.py:3548), so `do_check_health` runs it inside `transaction()` (cpersona/maintenance_handlers.py:148), and its repair calls `coarse_index.build_coarse_index(db, "memories")` on that connection (checks.py:3058). The build (cpersona/coarse_index.py:130) only reads the database: it scans `plan_rows`, streams every stored vector, then writes and fsyncs a file and calls `os.replace`. Every store, archive, queue drain, import and merge from every session waits behind it for a time that grows linearly with the corpus. This is the same call the recall coarse-index suggestion hands to agents. Reproduced: a concurrent single-row store waited for the build to finish.
issues.fix_sketch: Keep only detection in the locked run and build the coarse index after the commit on a read snapshot (`database.read_snapshot()`), so `plan_rows` and the vector stream still see one consistent snapshot without holding the write lock.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10; reproduced. Same class as bug-254 and bug-324 (read-only whole-database work under the write lock); the same call site also publishes uncommitted state, bug-643.
issues.fix_note: The coarse index's repair no longer builds inside check_health's locked fix run. run_health_checks only detects the checks in POST_COMMIT_REPAIRS under fix. do_check_health runs them again after the commit with after_commit=True, and _rebuild_coarse_index turns the change log on in a commit of its own, builds the file on database.read_snapshot(), and prunes the log afterwards (or stops it when no file reads it). No writer waits on the build, and a run that rolls back publishes nothing. Reverting the fix turns tests/test_2611a2_w08.py::test_bug550_the_coarse_repair_builds_while_other_writers_proceed, ::test_bug550_a_fix_run_inside_a_transaction_never_builds and ::test_bug643_a_fix_run_that_rolls_back_leaves_no_coarse_file_that_hides_a_row red. Dropping the log start turns the first one and tests/test_bug514_index_change_log.py::test_the_coarse_repair_builds_a_file_the_log_vouches_for red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) check_health(fix=true) fails its repairs with 'database is locked' as soon as another process writes to the same database file. The fix run opens with `SAVEPOINT health_run` (cpersona/checks.py:3625), which begins a deferred transaction, so the run's first read pins a WAL snapshot. When a repair then needs to write while another connection has written, SQLite returns SQLITE_BUSY at once, because the busy handler does not apply to a read-to-write upgrade on a stale snapshot, so the 5 s `busy_timeout` (cpersona/database.py:235) never helps. The per-check `ROLLBACK TO` (checks.py:3643) keeps the stale snapshot, and each failure is turned into a `check_crashed` finding. Reproduced with a separate OS process committing short single-row inserts: the fix run's repairs failed with 'database is locked' within about 10 ms and the rows stayed unrepaired, while the same run with no other writer repaired them all.
issues.fix_sketch: Take the write lock before the run's first read: issue `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` (which honours busy_timeout) before `SAVEPOINT health_run`, or have `transaction()` begin IMMEDIATE when it wraps a fix run; optionally retry a check that hits SQLITE_BUSY after a fresh immediate begin.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10; reproduced. The outer savepoint was introduced by the bug-361 fix.
issues.fix_note: Already fixed in 2.6.11a1: transaction() now begins IMMEDIATE (cpersona/database.py), so a fix run holds SQLite's write lock from its first read and another process waits or is refused before the run starts its repairs, instead of making every remaining repair fail with 'database is locked'. tests/test_2611a2_w08.py pins the health-run case (another connection tries to commit between the run's first read and its first repair); it turns red if the BEGIN IMMEDIATE is removed. Fixed in 2.6.11a1 by 75cf6fa ('Take SQLite's write lock when a write transaction starts'): transaction() issues BEGIN IMMEDIATE before the body runs, so check_health's fix run holds SQLite's write lock from its first read, and a repair never has to upgrade a stale snapshot. The busy_timeout applies, and another process waits instead of breaking the repair. Removing that BEGIN IMMEDIATE turns tests/test_2611a2_w08.py::test_bug551_repairs_converge_when_another_process_writes_after_the_runs_first_read red with check_crashed 'database is locked'.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) deep_check(fix=true) permanently deletes complete CJK memories as trivial content. `deep_short_content` selects rows with `LENGTH(TRIM(content)) <= 5` (cpersona/checks.py:138, 3798), and SQLite LENGTH counts characters, so a full Japanese statement of 3 to 5 characters is classed with acknowledgements like 'ok'. On fix the unlocked rows are deleted (checks.py:3816-3820). Reproduced through the real store handler and `do_deep_check(fix=True, checks=['short_content'])`: four complete Japanese facts of 3 to 5 characters were deleted together with 'ok' and 'hmm', while the English versions of the same facts survived. No user-facing text says the fix deletes rows: the deep_check description says only that fix=true applies repairs for short_content (cpersona/server.py:2494-2499), and docs/operations.md:441 recommends running `deep_check(agent_id, fix=true)` monthly.
issues.pattern: rows = \[r for r in candidates if _short_content_length\(r\[1\]\) <= _SHORT_CONTENT_THRESHOLD\]
issues.fix_sketch: Stop deep_check from deleting on a character count: make short_content report-only, or make the predicate script-aware (count tokens or bytes, or exempt CJK). Document in the tool description and docs that fix=true deletes rows.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10; reproduced. The fix changes deep_check's documented repair behaviour, so it needs a contract decision on what short_content may do under fix=true.
issues.fix_note: deep_short_content keeps the SQL LENGTH(TRIM) <= 5 prefilter and then applies _short_content_length, which counts each East Asian wide character as 3, so complete 2-5 character CJK facts are no longer reported or deleted as trivial while 'ok'/'hmm' still are. Reverting to the raw character count turns tests/test_2611a1_u09.py::test_short_content_repair_keeps_short_cjk_facts red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) deep_check's orphaned_episodes scan costs episodes times memories and runs on the shared request read connection. The bug-116 fix wraps both sides of the window test in `datetime()` (cpersona/checks.py:3850-3861), so the correlated `NOT EXISTS` cannot range-scan the timestamp column of `idx_memories_span`; the query plan uses the index on `agent_id` only, and each episode scans all of the agent's memories. `do_deep_check` runs this report-only check under `connection()` (cpersona/maintenance_handlers.py:352-353), the read connection that request reads share, so every recall, list or get_contents issued meanwhile waits for the statement. Reproduced: run time grew about 4x per doubling of episodes and memories, and a list_memories call for a different agent issued during the scan waited for it.
issues.fix_sketch: Run report-only deep checks on the background connection, and make the window test sargable, for example by normalising timestamps at write time or adding a normalised column the span index can range-scan.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10; reproduced. The non-sargable predicate was introduced by the bug-116 fix.
issues.fix_note: deep_orphaned_episodes reads the agent's datetime()-normalised memory times once, sorted, and binary-searches each episode window (same inclusive bounds and NULL semantics), instead of a correlated NOT EXISTS costing episodes x memories; do_deep_check runs report-only deep checks on background_connection(). Reverting the query turns tests/test_2611a2_w05.py::test_orphaned_episodes_cost_is_not_episodes_times_memories red; reverting the connection turns ::test_report_only_deep_checks_run_on_the_background_connection red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) Following the documented repair for `stale_scoring_version` erases every `set_recall_precision` override. When `CPERSONA_AUTO_CALIBRATE` and `CPERSONA_CALIBRATE_ON_MODEL_CHANGE` are both off and the sidecar has a stale scoring fingerprint, `ensure_calibrated_on_startup` returns `noop` (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:2231-2250) before the path that preloads stored betas. The overrides are therefore not applied: `get_recall_precision` shows `overridden: False`. Running `calibrate_threshold`, as docs/upgrading-to-2.6.md:57-59 directs, carries nothing forward, because `_stored_agent_maps_to_carry` returns `{}` for a stale fingerprint (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:1181-1182), and that includes `agent_betas`. The sidecar is rewritten with `agent_betas={}` and a fresh fingerprint (admin_handlers.py:1922), after which `deep_check` reports ok and nothing signals the loss. This contradicts docs/upgrading-to-2.6.md:64-65 ('Preferences set with `set_recall_precision` are kept') and the code's own comment that a scoring change does not invalidate a stated preference. Reproduced: overrides of 0.9 and 0.1 for two agents were permanently dropped from the sidecar.
issues.pattern: ^    # BEFORE the no-recalibration return below: a stale boot with recalibration disabled$
issues.fix_sketch: Carry `agent_betas` regardless of the scoring and dimension staleness test in `_stored_agent_maps_to_carry`, since betas are preferences and not measurements, or load the stored betas on the noop boot path too. Make the `stale_scoring_version` hint depend on whether recalibration on boot is enabled.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10. Reproduced. Related: bug-184, bug-189, and bug-650 (the restart hint on the same status).
issues.fix_note: ensure_calibrated_on_startup now preloads stored agent_betas (and claims the beta axis) whenever nothing was restored, before the no-recalibration return. A stale-scoring boot with recalibration disabled therefore applies the set_recall_precision overrides, and the next calibrate_threshold writes them back instead of an empty map. The stale_scoring_version hint names the config when boot will not recalibrate. If the move is reverted, tests/test_2611a1_u11.py::test_calibrate_after_a_noop_boot_keeps_the_precision_overrides and test_a_noop_boot_still_applies_the_stored_precision_overrides go red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) `deep_near_duplicate` builds a Python dict for every pair above `NEAR_DUPLICATE_COSINE`, then keeps only the first 20 (cpersona/checks.py:3999-4017). `NEAR_DUPLICATE_ROW_CAP` (default 5000, cpersona/config.py:429) bounds the row count but not the pair count, so memory is quadratic on a clustered corpus. Templated content that differs only by a counter is not skipped as an exact duplicate. The computation is synchronous numpy and Python on the event loop. Reproduced with 768-d vectors at cosine about 0.997: peak RSS rose by 167 MB at 1000 rows, 648 MB at 2000 and 1.46 GB at 3000 (about 325 bytes per pair), and the event loop was blocked for 5.3 s at 3000 rows. Extrapolated to the 5000-row cap, that is about 4 GB, against the roughly 266 MB budget the cap's comment states.
issues.fix_sketch: Count qualifying pairs with a vectorised mask and build dicts only for the top 20 (for example argpartition over the upper-triangle values above the threshold), without materialising every pair. Run the computation off the event loop with `asyncio.to_thread`.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10. Reproduced. The trigger needs thousands of mutually near-identical rows among one agent's newest records, such as templated or periodic memories.
issues.fix_note: deep_near_duplicate counts each row's pairs above the threshold with a vectorised mask (exact-content duplicates excluded by a label comparison) and keeps only a running top 20 under the old sample order. It builds no dict per pair, and it runs in asyncio.to_thread off the event loop. Reverting to the dict-per-pair loop turns tests/test_2611a2_w05.py::test_near_duplicate_memory_does_not_grow_with_pairs red; removing to_thread turns ::test_near_duplicate_compares_off_the_event_loop red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The `python -m cpersona.checkup` CLI, documented as the form to use in CI (docs/tools.md:78-79), never installs an embedding client. `_run` (cpersona/checkup.py:127-142) calls `do_check_health` and `do_deep_check` with `vector._embedding_client` unset. Three checks change their answer as a result. `check_embedding_dimension` returns `[]` (cpersona/checks.py:441-442), so mixed embedding widths go unreported. `_null_embedding_severity` demotes NULL embeddings to info (checks.py:541). `_reembeddable` reports 0 repairable (checks.py:598). Reproduced on one database seeded with two 64-d rows, two 8-d rows and six NULL rows, with `CPERSONA_EMBEDDING_MODE=http`: `checkup --json --strict` exited 0 as healthy with four info findings. The MCP `check_health` with a client reported `embedding_dimension_mismatch` and `null_embedding` as critical and exits 2 under strict. The NULL-embedding demotion is partly disclosed by the bug-428 docstring, but the dimension axis is skipped silently, and the hint's advice to restart CPersona does not apply to a CLI process.
issues.fix_sketch: When `EMBEDDING_MODE` is not none, have checkup build the same embedding client that server startup builds. Otherwise, have the client-dependent critical checks emit a 'not verified, no embedding client in this process' finding that fails under --strict instead of returning nothing. Make the null_embedding hint name the CLI context.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10. Reproduced. Related: bug-428 and bug-354 (the same class: an axis that cannot be verified is reported as clean).
issues.fix_note: checkup._run installs the embedding client the server would build (shared vector.build_embedding_client) before running do_check_health/do_deep_check, and restores the previous singleton afterwards; an unsupported mode exits 2. Reverting it turns test_checkup_reports_dimension_drift_and_null_backlog_like_check_health and test_checkup_fix_reembeds_through_the_configured_backend in tests/test_2611a2_w07.py red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) One record with a numeric-string timestamp blocks the coarse index build for every agent. The store path accepts any timestamp string (cpersona/memory_handlers.py:199). For a value such as '2025' or '0', SQLite `datetime()` returns a negative-year value like '-4707-06-10 12:00:00'. `build_coarse_index` declines the whole build, whose plan is corpus-wide, when a value is not canonical (cpersona/coarse_index.py:153-160). `check_invalid_timestamp` counts only `datetime(timestamp) IS NULL` (checks.py:1867-1871), and `timestamp_format_drift` reports the row as info with repairable 0. A full `check_health(fix=True)` therefore leaves the row in place, while `check_coarse_index` keeps claiming the index is repairable, so the suggested fix fails every time. Reproduced: one row from a second agent with timestamp '2025' made the build return `built: False` before and after a full fix run, and a canonical control built normally. In the default auto cue mode the time cue's remainder is then never searched for any agent. Answers stay correct, but reach and latency suffer.
issues.pattern: if value is None or not vector_index\._is_canonical\(value\):
issues.fix_sketch: Treat a non-canonical `datetime(timestamp)` result like NULL and store `UNREADABLE_TIMESTAMP` for that row instead of declining the whole build. Separately, widen `invalid_timestamp`, or validate at store time, so that values `datetime()` maps outside years 0000-9999 are caught.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10. Reproduced. `created_at` already gets the opposite treatment: a non-canonical row is excluded rather than declining the build (cpersona/vector_index.py:254-258).
issues.fix_note: A datetime(timestamp) that is NULL or not canonical (a negative year, e.g. from a bare number such as '2025') is stored as UNREADABLE_TIMESTAMP instead of declining the server-wide build. Such a value sorts below every canonical bound, so it falls in no period, as in SQL. coarse_search._from_index hands a period with a non-canonical (negative-year) lower bound to the live store, where SQL's text comparison could admit those rows. If either part is reverted, tests/test_2611a1_u06.py::test_one_negative_year_timestamp_does_not_block_the_coarse_build fails.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) Concurrent index builds share one fixed temp path that is opened with O_TRUNC. Both `build_coarse_index` (cpersona/coarse_index.py:186) and `vector_index.build_index` (cpersona/vector_index.py:361) write to `f"{out}.tmp"` through `fileperms.open_private`, which opens with O_CREAT and O_TRUNC but not O_EXCL (cpersona/fileperms.py:108-110). The asyncio write lock serialises builds only inside one server process. Nothing serialises the CLI build against a server's `check_health(coarse_index, fix=true)`, or two server processes on one database. Reproduced with two builds on separate connections against one output path: build A published the file and reported 1500 rows. Build B failed its rename with FileNotFoundError. The published file had B's header and size, so it passed the exact size check in `load_coarse_index` (coarse_index.py:268), yet 1024 of 1501 rows held bits that did not match the stored vectors. The damage is silent but confined to a derived, rebuildable file. For the coarse index it means wrong candidate selection. The contiguous vector index shares the pattern, where it would give wrong scores.
issues.fix_sketch: Create the temp file with a unique name per call (for example `tempfile.mkstemp` in the output directory, reopened through fileperms, as bug-350 did for export) in both builders. Optionally take an advisory lock file so that a concurrent build is refused rather than raced.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10. Reproduced, with the interleaving forced inside one process; the same file semantics apply across processes. The second site is cpersona/vector_index.py:361. Related: bug-350.
issues.fix_note: build_coarse_index, and vector_index.build_index at the same line shape, write through a per-call mkstemp temp file in the output directory (fileperms.temp_beside) instead of the shared `<out>.tmp`, and their existing cleanup now removes only that file. If either is reverted, the matching parameter of tests/test_2611a1_u06.py::test_two_record_index_builds_at_once_publish_a_whole_file fails (the second build raises FileNotFoundError).

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The coarse-index `suggestion` on recall, and the `time_cue.remainder` hint, propose a fix call that `check_health` declines. `coarse_notice.notice` checks only that the cue mode is auto and that `records - window` reaches `INDEX_MATTERS_ROWS` (cpersona/coarse_notice.py:55-61). `records` is an unfiltered `COUNT(*)` from `scope_stats.get_pool_counts` (cpersona/memory_handlers.py:2505, 3189). `check_coarse_index` counts only embedded rows and returns nothing when `far_rows` is 0 (cpersona/checks.py:2947-2955), or when no index exists and `far_rows < INDEX_MATTERS_ROWS` (checks.py:2988-2990). Reproduced under the default `CPERSONA_EMBEDDING_MODE=none`: a scope past the window received the suggestion. The fix call returned healthy and built nothing, and the next session received the same suggestion. The remainder hint (`CUE_REMAINDER_HINT`, memory_handlers.py:1998-2002) fires when one embedded row lies past the cap, so it names a no-op whenever 0 < far_rows < 1000. The suggestion also ignores `source_id` scoping and remote search, from the same predicate mismatch (not separately reproduced). docs/tools.md:92-96 calls the suggestion's fix the call that builds the index.
issues.fix_sketch: Give `notice()` and the remainder hint the check's own predicate: count embedded rows only, scoped like the cue arm including `source_id`, and stay silent when there is no local vector search (no client, or remote search). Let `check_coarse_index` under fix=True build whenever the index is absent and `far_rows` is greater than 0.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10. Reproduced for the no-embeddings case and for the remainder hint; the `source_id` and remote-search variants were confirmed by reading only.
issues.fix_note: recall now builds the coarse suggestion through coarse_notice.scope_notice. It is silent without a local vector search, and it counts embedded rows in the cue arm's own scope (source_id included), the same predicate the check that builds the index uses. Reverting it to notice(pool_memories, ...) turns test_no_suggestion_without_an_embedding_client, test_no_suggestion_under_remote_vector_search, test_the_suggestion_counts_embedded_rows_only and test_the_suggestion_counts_the_recalls_own_source red. The companion change is cpersona/checks.py `if far_rows < INDEX_MATTERS_ROWS and not fix:` (builds under fix below the line). Reverting that turns test_the_remainder_hint_names_a_call_that_builds red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The coarse index path reads its whole live tail in one unbounded fetch. `_from_index` (cpersona/coarse_search.py:266-269) calls `vector._index_tail_rows` with `scan_limit=-1`. `_index_tail_rows` (cpersona/vector.py:963-971) then runs one `execute_fetchall` over every row past the index watermark, plus the named holes, within the agent's axes and the optional period. The fetch includes every embedding blob, and the rows at scan positions below `start`, which can never be candidates, are read too. Nothing rebuilds the index automatically, so the tail only grows after a build. The `coarse_index_tail_grown` finding is info-level, so nothing warns. Each cue recall in the default auto mode, and every recall when far seats are enabled, then pays memory and time that grow with index staleness, more than the chunked live supplier (`_from_live`, coarse_search.py:202-210, `fetchmany(VECTOR_SCAN_CHUNK_ROWS)`) it is meant to undercut. This contradicts the design note that the default cue mode's cost does not grow with the store. Reproduced on a scratch store: with 8,000 rows added after the build, the index path peaked at about 21 MB against 1.9 MB for the live path, and returned the same candidates.
issues.pattern: found = await _rank\(db, index, selected, tail, query_bits, dim, k, start, end\)
issues.fix_sketch: Read the tail through a cursor in `VECTOR_SCAN_CHUNK_ROWS` chunks, as `_from_live` does: fetch ids and `created_at` first to place the rows, then read blobs only for rows inside `[start, end)`. Alternatively, treat a tail past a bound (for example a ratio of the indexed count) as unable to answer, and raise `coarse_index_tail_grown` to a warning.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10 and reproduced. Related to bug-329, which bounded the gather temporaries on the other scan paths.
issues.fix_note: The coarse supplier's index path now builds the tail statement (vector._index_tail_statement) and _rank reads it through a cursor in VECTOR_SCAN_CHUNK_ROWS chunks. Each row is placed, then ranked or dropped as it arrives, and only one int64 per row is kept for the index rows' places. Peak memory no longer grows with the rows written since the build. Reverting to vector._index_tail_rows(..., scan_limit=-1) plus the synchronous _rank turns all 8 cases of test_the_index_reads_the_rows_since_its_build_in_chunks red (one read handed back 40 stored vectors, against a chunk of 4).

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) An empty `CPERSONA_DB_PATH` is not treated as unset. cpersona/config.py:67 reads it with `os.environ.get(key, default)`, so a variable that is present but empty yields `''`. SQLite opens `''` as a private temporary database that is discarded on close, and each `aiosqlite.connect('')` gets a different one. The write connection (cpersona/database.py:1145) migrates its own schema, while each reader (`_open_reader`, database.py:1049) opens a fresh empty database. The server starts with no warning, then every store and recall fails with `no such table`, and anything written is lost at exit. An MCP client config or installer form that passes the variable with an empty value triggers it. The same empty-value hole exists in the embedding mode chain at config.py:605: an empty `CPERSONA_EMBEDDING_MODE` falls through to `EMBEDDING_MODE`, and if that is also empty the result is `''`, which the startup check refuses although the documented default is `none`. Reproduced by running the startup order and then the store and recall handlers.
issues.fix_sketch: Treat an empty value as unset, for example `os.environ.get("CPERSONA_DB_PATH") or "data/cpersona.db"`, matching the rule the other parsers in the module already apply. Apply the same rule to the embedding mode fallback chain.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10 and reproduced. These two reads are sites the bug-133 empty-means-default rule did not reach.
issues.fix_note: DB_PATH and the EMBEDDING_MODE fallback chain treat an empty value as unset (`or` default), the rule the bug-133 parsers apply. An empty CPERSONA_DB_PATH no longer opens SQLite's per-connection temporary database. If this is reverted, tests/test_2611a1_u11.py::test_an_empty_db_path_falls_back_to_the_default goes red. If the EMBEDDING_MODE chain is reverted, test_an_empty_embedding_mode_falls_back_to_the_default[--none] goes red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) A malformed forced reconstruct setting becomes an active operator override instead of staying unset. `CPERSONA_RECONSTRUCT_FORCED_COUNT` and `CPERSONA_RECONSTRUCT_FORCED_BUDGET` are documented as unset by default (docs/configuration.md), and unset means no override. When the variable is present but does not parse, cpersona/config.py:249-253 falls back to a concrete 1, and config.py:305-310 falls back to `RECONSTRUCT_DEFAULT_BUDGET` (4000). A value of 0 for the forced count also becomes a forced 1. `validate_reconstruct_counts` accepts both, so the server starts and logs only that it is using default 1. Every reconstruct call for every agent is then pinned to at most one item, or to a 4000-character budget, and a forced budget also disables pro mode's uncapped path (cpersona/reconstruct.py:1531). This contradicts the module's own rule that an unreadable value falls back to the setting's documented default. Reproduced: `CPERSONA_RECONSTRUCT_FORCED_COUNT=5x` gave a forced count of 1 and `FORCED_BUDGET=8k` gave 4000.
issues.fix_sketch: Parse the forced settings so that an unparseable value falls back to None (unset), with a warning that the override is ignored. Make a malformed default count fall back to `min(10, MAX_COUNT)`, as when it is unset.
issues.note: Found by the 2026-10-13 audit of 2.6.10 and reproduced. Related to bug-133 (fallback rule for malformed values) and bug-321.
issues.fix_note: Forced reconstruct count and budget are read with _parse_optional_int: a value that does not parse is ignored (stays None, no operator override) with a warning, and a malformed DEFAULT_COUNT falls back to min(10, MAX_COUNT) like an unset one.
